title: Meta releases Muse Spark Open — 816B-parameter weights that run on a Mac
subtitle: The open-weight version of Meta's Muse Spark family targets Apple silicon, with a 1-million-token context and a license that permits commercial use with restrictions.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Meta published Muse Spark Open to Hugging Face on October 15, 2026, releasing the first open-weight entry in its Muse Spark line. The model is a 816-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts with 42 billion active parameters per token and a 1-million-token context window. The weights ship under the Muse Model License, which permits commercial use but imposes a monthly-active-user ceiling and attribution requirements rather than being a true permissive license like Apache 2.0.

The target deployment is unusual for a frontier-scale model. Meta tuned the release for local inference on Apple silicon — specifically, M-series Macs with Unified Memory large enough to hold the active expert set in RAM. That shifts the economics for a developer or a small team: a workstation with 128 GB or more of unified memory can run the model without a GPU cluster or an API bill. The hosted Muse Spark 1.3 remains available for teams that want managed inference.

This release is a response to a specific competitive gap. Chinese labs — Qwen, DeepSeek, and Zhipu among them — have spent the year dominating the open-weight leaderboards while US frontier labs stayed closed. Meta's own prior Muse Spark releases were API-only, and the July 2026 round of coverage specifically noted that no downloadable weights had been published. Reversing that choice, at the top end of Meta's model stack, puts an American lab back in a conversation it had largely ceded.

Takeaway for learners: open-weight does not mean unconstrained, and license terms are now where real policy work is happening. Before you build on Muse Spark Open — or any lab's open-weight release — read the license and the acceptable-use policy carefully. The MAU ceiling, the attribution clause, and the fine print on competitive use will decide whether what you build is actually permitted, not the headline parameter count.
